changes.after: Use compiler messages and runtime checks without treating them as proof that every path is safe.

before:
Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic to request useful GCC diagnostics. They do not mean every possible warning is enabled. This course also uses -Werror, which treats emitted warnings as build errors rather than silently accepting them.

Save the complete safe example below as main.cpp in a disposable folder. With GCC installed, these terminal commands build it with the stated warning policy and then run it on Linux or macOS:
```sh
g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.cpp -o example
./example
```
The output is 2 4. These commands do not install a compiler.

A local build with -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can instrument checks for supported memory and undefined-behavior errors. It only checks paths that actually execute; a clean run does not prove the whole program safe. Tool availability and platform support matter.

On a platform whose GCC supports these sanitizers, build the same safe source into a separate executable:
```sh
g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined main.cpp -o checked
./checked
```
Its normal program output is still 2 4; sanitizer diagnostics, if any, must be investigated. A platform limitation is not a passing safety test.

The worked array iteration stays in bounds. We do not execute invalid indexing or dangling-pointer examples. To demonstrate a rejected build safely, the changed case adds a genuinely unused variable; the configured warning policy rejects it before any run.
Expected output or behavior: 2 4 . Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Build the safe worked example with sanitizer instrumentation locally, then record both the flags and what paths you actually tested. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A diagnostic is a compiler message about your code. GCC's -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic options request useful warnings. They do not enable every possible warning. -Werror makes emitted warnings fail the build.

Save the example as main.cpp. With GCC installed, build it using g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.cpp -o example. After a successful build, run ./example on Linux or macOS, or .\example.exe in Windows PowerShell.

A sanitizer adds runtime checks for certain errors. On a supported GCC platform, adding -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can help detect memory errors and undefined behavior on executed paths. These options do not install the required tools.
The program prints 2 4, with a space after each number. A failed build is not a successful run, even if an older executable remains in the folder.
A clean sanitizer run only covers the paths it checked. It does not prove every possible execution is safe. A missing or unsupported sanitizer is also not a passing check.

before.question: With this course’s -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror flags, add int unused = 7; inside main and never use it. What should you do with the build result?
choices: Treat the warning-as-error failure as a rejected build; no run is certified.
Assume compilation succeeded because unused variables can never matter.
Run an out-of-bounds access to make the warning go away.
before.explanation: GCC diagnoses the unused local, and -Werror makes that diagnostic a compilation failure. Fix the cause or justify a deliberate policy change; do not pretend a binary was produced.

after.question: With GCC's -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror options, add an unused int unused = 7 inside main. How should the result be handled?
choices: Treat the warning made into an error as a failed build and fix its cause.
Assume the build succeeded because unused variables never matter.
Read outside the array to remove the warning.
after.explanation: GCC warns about the unused local variable. -Werror makes that warning fail the build, so the changed program has not been successfully built.
